text: The Bobbili Fort, situated in the Vizianagaram district of Andhra Pradesh, was constructed in the middle of the 19th century by Chinna Ranga Rao and his successors, following their improved economic conditions. It stands on the site of a previous mud fort of the same name, which was destroyed during the Bobbili war in 1757, a conflict between the Rajas of Bobbili and the Maharaja of Vizianagaram. Chinna Ranga Rao, who survived the Battle of Bobbili as a child, was later installed as the Raja of Bobbili, and his lineage built the present fort after regaining control of the kingdom. The fort covers an area of 10 acres (4.0 ha) and features an impressive entrance gate in Indo-Saracenic architectural style with a high dome and includes four major palaces, a Durbar Hall, two temples, and multiple mantapas. The fort complex spans 40,000 square feet (3,700 m²), with the Raja's palace being the largest and three-storeyed. The Durbar Hall served as the venue for crowning ceremonies. The two temples—one dedicated to Venugopala Swamy, established at the founding of Bobbili, and another built by Chinna Ranga Rao after he regained his territory—include a Gopura constructed in 1851 and a Vasant Mandapa built in 1825 by Maharaja Krishna Das Ranga Rao. The Pooja Mahal and Prangmahal, a well-preserved residence of the Raja decorated with tapestries, paintings, and porcelain, are also part of the complex. Bobbili is 55 kilometres (34 mi) from Vizianagaram, connected by rail and road, with Vizianagaram being the nearest railway station on the Raipur-Vizianagaram line, and a bridge across the Vedavati River providing access. The history of Bobbili dates back to 1652 when Sher Muhammad Khan, Fouzdar of the Nawab of Srikakulam, accompanied by Peddarayadu, the 15th scion of the Rajas of Venkatagiri, and Pusapati Madhava Varma, ancestor of the Vijayanagram family, arrived in the Vizianagaram district. In one version, the Nawab granted land to Peddarayadu, who built a fort named "Bobbili" (meaning "the royal tiger") in appreciation; in another, Rayudu's son Lingappa chose Bobbili as his capital, named it "Pedda-puli" (meaning "big tiger"), which evolved into Bobbili. During this period, Sher Khan's son was abducted and rescued by Lingappa, who was then granted 12 villages and the title "Ranga Rao." Lingappa was succeeded by Vengal Ranga Rao, then Rangapati, then Rayadappa, whose adopted son Gopalakrishna succeeded him. A Muslim saint had warned the royal brothers against building the fort, but they ignored the warning. In 1753, the Nizam of Hyderabad gave Northern Circars to the French, and General Charles Bussy leased Chicacole and Rajahmundry to Pedda Viziarama Raju, the Maharaja of Vizianagaram, leading to a rift with the Nizam. In 1756, a rebellion among local chieftains prompted General Bussy to attack with 11,000 troops from the Raja of Vizianagaram, who instigated him by falsely claiming the Raja of Bobbili was behind the rebellion. It is said the Raja bribed his interpreters to persuade Bussy to move the Raja of Bobbili away from the fort. Bussy offered pardon and land elsewhere, but this was rejected. He then attacked the fort, breached the mud fort with cannons, and took control. Upon entering, he found dead bodies scattered throughout, and an old man handed him a child believed to be the son of the deceased Raja. The Raja of Vizianagaram rejoiced by entering the city and hoisting the French flag, but three days later, his camp was attacked by three Bobbili men, including Tandra Paparayudu, who killed him and committed suicide. As of 24 January 1757, survivors were Vengal Ranga Rao (Chinna Ranga Rao) and his infant son. They fled to Bhadrachalam and, in 1759, were offered their old holdings by Ananda Raju of Vizianagaram at Masulipatam in the presence of Colonel Forde, receiving the Kavit and Rajam taluks and the fort area for an annuity lease of Rs 20,000. Vengal Ranga Rao died three years later, and his son lived for two years before being succeeded by Chinna Ranga Rao (also known as Venkata Ranga Rao). In 1766, Sitaram, the new Raja of Vizianagaram, arrested Chinna Ranga Rao and imprisoned him in Vizianagaram's fort. He escaped in 1790, sought protection in Hyderabad, and in 1794 regained his property due to the splintering of the Vizianagaram zamindari. Chinna Ranga Rao then adopted Rayadappa as his son. After his death in 1801, efforts to merge Bobbili with Vizianagaram failed, and a lasting settlement was made with Rayadappa and his son Svetachalapti, who ruled until 1862. In 1891, a stone monument was erected to commemorate the Bobbili tragedy. The fort was built in the Indo-Saracenic style, likely favored during the exile of Ranga Rao and his son in Hyderabad, where they lived for over a decade and a half. Chinna Ranga Rao constructed the oldest part of the main palace with Saracenic arches. However, in 1861, a report by the Acting District Engineer to the Chief Secretary noted the stone fort lacked adequate defense capability. The fort's facade resembles a palace with high walls, up to 20 feet (6.1 m) tall, rather than a castle.
